intent: Two islands less than four kilometres apart, with the International Date Line between them, so one is almost a full day ahead of the other; one is a US village, the other a Russian military post.
pacing_profile: documentary: cold open, place, why in 2–5 beats, twist, close answers the open, short CTA (docs/STORY_GUIDELINES.md §2)
pause_policy: Pause only at the marked ellipses.
title: The island where you can see tomorrow

lines.direction: tight on the village shore, a figure waves, the pull-out reveals the second island right there
lines.text: From this beach, you can look across the water and see tomorrow.

lines.direction: the gap line draws from the village to the Russian island; counter on the distance; Russia fills in solid
lines.text: This is Little Diomede, an American village in the Bering Strait. That is Big Diomede, Russian territory, just 3.8 kilometres away.

lines.direction: the dashed line draws down the strait between the islands; TODAY and TOMORROW tags stamp either side; card with the 21-hour gap
lines.text: Between them runs the International Date Line. Cross it, and the calendar jumps. Big Diomede is 21 hours ahead.

lines.direction: figures stand on Big Diomede, get crossed out and vanish; the tags come off; the camera drifts west toward the mainland
lines.text: Nobody lives on the Russian side any more. Its villagers were moved to the mainland in 1948, and today only a border post and a weather station remain.

lines.direction: back to the village; figures pop in on the US shore and wave at the Russian island; the gap line redraws
lines.text: On the American side, about 80 people still live in the village, facing Russia, facing tomorrow, across water you could row in an hour.

lines.direction: answer the opening line with the same noun
lines.text: Two islands, one short row apart, and tomorrow is always on the other side of the water.

lines.direction: short follow — the outro visual does the work
lines.text: Follow for a new map story every day.
